body.heading: Parents apologising is not weakness
paragraphs: When a parent says “I was wrong to shout; I’m sorry,” a child learns something no lecture can teach: that authority and accountability can live in the same person. Far from undermining respect, it is one of the main ways respect is built.
Keep it clean, though — an apology that ends with “…but you did push me” hands the fault back at the last second. Children notice the hand-back every time.

body.heading: Between partners, between siblings
paragraphs: The household’s emotional weather is set by whether its adults can repair in the open. Small, prompt, ungrudging apologies between partners teach everyone watching that conflict is survivable and love is not withdrawn as punishment.
Siblings, meanwhile, need apologies that are not extracted like confessions. A forced “sorry” teaches performance; a modelled one teaches the real thing, eventually.

body.heading: Sorry, then the change
paragraphs: Every apology at home should end in one small visible change: the raised voice replaced by a pause, the slammed door by a walked-away minute. The change is the apology’s proof of postage.
Homes where apologies are normal are not homes without conflict. They are homes where conflict has a known way back — and everyone knows the way.

takeaway: Apologise cleanly at home, model it for the young, and let one small change prove it.
